title: Forest garden: the ground cover layer
subtitle: Low-growing plants that protect the soil and provide harvest from the forest floor.
excerpt: The ground cover layer in a forest garden keeps the soil covered and active under shrubs and trees. A good ground cover mixture suppresses weeds, reduces water loss, and provides a harvest at soil level. It is established in years three to five once the woody plants are in.
sourceNotes: Ground cover layer framework from Martin Crawford, Creating a Forest Garden (2010). Species selection from Plants For A Future database (pfaf.org) and Agroforestry Research Trust species data.

glossaryTerms.definition: In a forest garden, the lowest layer of plants: low-growing perennials, bulbs, and spreading groundcover plants that grow under shrubs and trees. The ground cover layer prevents bare soil, suppresses annual weeds, and provides a harvest from the forest floor. It is the last layer established in a developing forest garden.

content.text: is the last to establish in a forest garden. It is planted once the canopy and shrub layers have created enough shade and the soil quality has improved. In the early years of a forest garden, annual vegetables fill this role; perennial ground cover takes over as the system matures.

Wild garlic naturalises in damp shade and provides a spring harvest. Creeping Jenny (not edible, but excellent groundcover) fills gaps in deep shade. Strawberries work on the sunnier ground cover edges. Viola odorata (sweet violet) is edible and spreads by runners to fill bare ground.

Plant ground cover in year three or four, once the shrub layer is establishing and providing some shade. Before that, the open ground is too competitive for low-growing perennials to establish well. Bulbs (wild garlic, bluebell, snowdrop) can go in earlier: they are dormant in summer and do not compete with young plants growing through summer.

Ground cover plants that self-seed or spread by runners (wild garlic, violets, strawberries) will move into areas where they are not wanted. Manage by pulling seedlings from paths and beds each spring. A ground cover layer in a forest garden is never truly weed-free; the goal is to keep it manageable and diverse.
